topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Secret Whisper for Contact Tracing
target_audience: University students (Computer Science, Data Privacy, or Public Health Tech)

outline.topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Secret Whisper for Contact Tracing
outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science, Data Privacy, or Public Health Tech)

sections.title: The Privacy Dilemma: The Health vs. Privacy Trade-off
sections.content: Introduce the challenge of tracking a virus without creating a 'Big Brother' surveillance state. Define the goal: How can Bob know he was exposed to Alice without a central server knowing where Alice and Bob were or who they are?
sections.example: Visual: Two characters, Alice and Bob, walking in a park. A central 'Eye' (Server) tries to watch them, but DP-3T puts a fog between the Eye and the citizens.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Cryptographic Hashes & BLE
sections.content: Briefly explain two building blocks: 1. One-way Hash Functions (transforming data into a unique string that can't be reversed). 2. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) 'Beacons' (short-range digital handshakes).
sections.example: Visual: A 'Meat Grinder' icon representing the Hash function. Input 'Secret' -> Output 'f3a2...'. Show a smartphone emitting a small blue ripple to represent a BLE beacon.

sections.title: Step 1: Local Key Generation (The Secret Seed)
sections.content: Explain the hierarchy of keys generated locally on the phone. Every day, a phone generates a Temporary Exposure Key (TEK). From this, it derives Rolling Proximity Identifiers (RPIs) that change every 15 minutes to prevent tracking.
sections.example: Graphic: A 'Tree' diagram. Root = Secret Key (SK). Branch = Daily Key (TEK). Leaves = RPI_1, RPI_2... RPI_n (changing like a digital camouflage).

sections.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake (Whispering in the Crowd)
sections.content: When Alice and Bob are near each other, their phones exchange RPIs via Bluetooth. They store these 'random-looking' numbers locally on their own devices. No location data or names are exchanged.
sections.example: Visual: Alice's phone sends 'ID_Alpha' to Bob. Bob's phone sends 'ID_Beta' to Alice. Both phones save these IDs in a local 'Digital Diary' that stays on the phone.

sections.title: Step 3: Notification & Decentralized Matching
sections.content: If Alice tests positive, she voluntarily uploads her Daily Keys (TEKs) to a public server. Bob’s phone periodically downloads these keys. Bob’s phone then locally recalculates the possible RPIs from those keys and checks if they match any IDs in his 'Digital Diary'.
sections.example: Animation: Alice uploads a 'Key' to a cloud. Bob's phone downloads it and runs a 'Match' process. If a match is found, Bob sees a 'Risk of Exposure' alert, but the server never knows Bob was the one who matched it.

sections.title: Summary: Why it Works
sections.content: Recap the decentralized nature: The server only acts as a 'bulletin board' for keys. The actual 'matching' happens on the user's device, ensuring the government never knows who met whom.
sections.example: Conclusion Image: A shield protecting a group of people. The text overlay: 'Decentralized = Privacy by Design'.

storyboard.title: The Privacy Dilemma: The Health vs. Privacy Trade-off
lecture_lines: Tracking virus spread is vital for public health safety.
Standard GPS tracking risks creating a mass surveillance state.
DP-3T offers contact tracing without sacrificing individual privacy.
animations: Show a network of blue circles (#0000FF) with red lines (#FF0000) appearing between them to show spread.
A large white eye icon (#FFFFFF) [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/eye.svg] appears at the top, sending yellow beams (#FFFF00) to every blue circle.
A green shield (#00FF00) [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/shield.svg] appears around each circle, and the yellow beams from the eye bounce off.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Cryptographic Hashes & BLE
lecture_lines: Cryptographic hashes turn data into irreversible unique strings.
Bluetooth Low Energy allows devices to exchange short-range signals.
These beacons act as proximity-based digital handshakes between users.
animations: A grey 'Meat Grinder' icon (#888888) takes in 'Secret' text and outputs a white hex string (#FFFFFF).
Two phone icons (#0000FF) emit pulsating light-blue ripples (#ADD8E6) towards each other.
When ripples meet, a small white handshake icon (#FFFFFF) appears between the phones.

storyboard.title: Step 1: Local Key Generation (The Secret Seed)
lecture_lines: Your phone generates a secret key stored only locally.
Every day, it derives a unique Temporary Exposure Key.
From this, it creates Rotating Proximity Identifiers (RPIs).
RPIs change every fifteen minutes to prevent tracking users.
No personal identity is ever linked to these random IDs.
animations: A blue phone icon (#0000FF) [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] shows a gold key (#FFD700) inside its screen.
The gold key generates a slightly different silver key (#C0C0C0) labeled 'Daily Key'.
The silver key shoots out 3 small white dots (#FFFFFF) labeled 'RPI-1', 'RPI-2', 'RPI-3'.
'RPI-1' fades out, 'RPI-2' becomes bold yellow (#FFFF00), then fades as 'RPI-3' becomes bold yellow.
A white 'Person' silhouette (#FFFFFF) appears far from the RPI dots, with a red 'X' (#FF0000) between them.

storyboard.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake (Whispering in the Crowd)
lecture_lines: Alice and Bob's phones exchange random RPIs via Bluetooth.
These IDs look like noise to any outside observer.
Each phone keeps a private diary of IDs seen nearby.
No location data or names are ever exchanged or saved.
The data stays on the device and is never uploaded.
animations: Phone A (#0000FF) sends a blue dot to Phone B (#00FF00), while Phone B sends a green dot to Phone A.
The dots transform into grey random characters like '7x!9?' (#AAAAAA) as they travel between phones.
Both phones show a white 'Diary' icon (#FFFFFF); Alice's diary stores the green dot.
Red text 'GPS: OFF' and 'NAME: HIDDEN' (#FF0000) appears above both phones.
An arrow points from the Diary to the phone's center; a distant white 'Cloud' (#FFFFFF) is crossed out in red.

storyboard.title: Step 3: Notification & Decentralized Matching
lecture_lines: If Alice tests positive, she uploads her daily keys.
These keys are shared on a public bulletin board server.
Bob's phone downloads new keys and regenerates possible RPIs.
Bob's phone checks for matches in its local diary.
The system alerts Bob privately without notifying the government.
animations: Alice's blue phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] (#0000FF) sends a silver 'Daily Key' (#C0C0C0) up to a white Cloud icon (#FFFFFF).
The Cloud transforms into a white grid (bulletin board) showing several silver keys.
Bob's green phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] (#00FF00) pulls a silver key from the board and generates white RPI dots (#FFFFFF) locally.
Bob's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] compares the new white RPI dots with its Diary; one pair flashes bright green (#00FF00).
A red exclamation mark (#FF0000) appears on Bob's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg]; no signal is sent back to the Cloud.

storyboard.title: Summary: Why it Works
lecture_lines: The server only acts as a public key repository.
Matching happens locally, ensuring true privacy by design.
DP-3T proves health tracking doesn't require mass surveillance.
animations: Show a central grey server icon (#888888) with the label 'Passive Storage' in white.
A white magnifying glass icon (#FFFFFF) appears over [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg], showing internal checkmark symbols.
A large green checkmark (#00FF00) appears over the entire scene with text 'Privacy Secured'.
